Circum Quadri

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: Four dots on a circle make a shape with four sides around it; four lines drawn across it always meet in one spot.
How to play: Drag a dot with a mouse or finger, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Press Check the theorem to find the meeting spot.
Look for the math

Move any dot around the circle and the four-sided shape changes completely. Yet two lines joining opposite corners and two lines joining opposite dots still cross at one point. The original page states exactly this, and the logic test checks it.

A shape wrapped around a circle

At each dot there is just one line that touches the circle without cutting it: the tangent. Two neighbouring tangents cross at a corner of a quadrilateral, so each of its four sides touches the circle. Here the dots are called A, B, C, D and the corners are P, Q, R, S. The original page calls the corners A, B, C, D and the touch points E, F, G, H: its line EG is our AC, its FH is our BD, and its diagonals are our PR and QS.

Why all four lines meet

Where the original page's diagonal AC meets the line EG at a point N, the two triangles AEN and CGN share an angle and have equal angles at E and G, because the tangents at the ends of a chord make equal angles with the chord. Comparing their areas two ways gives

AN / CN = AE / CG

So EG cuts the diagonal in the ratio of the two tangent lengths AE and CG. The same argument for FH gives AH / CF. But AE = AH and CG = CF, since two tangents drawn from one point to a circle are equal. Both lines cut the diagonal at the very same point. Doing it again for the other diagonal puts that point at the crossing of the diagonals: all four lines pass through M. The logic test checks both ratios, not just the meeting point, on every arrangement where they are well defined.

A bigger theorem

This is Brianchon's theorem with six tangents collapsed to four: two pairs of touch points pulled together leave a quadrilateral, and the three lines through opposite corners of the old hexagon become the diagonals and chords drawn here. The original page also mentions Ceva's theorem and a pole and polar argument; both work for any conic, not just a circle. This port draws the circle case the Java applet drew.

What the test checked

The logic test reproduces the applet's own circle, tangents and line crossings from its bytecode, then compares them with this page on the starting diagram and more than eight hundred other arrangements, including crossed and tightly clustered dots. Every side stays a tangent and all four lines meet, with an error below 1e-11 times the size of the drawing. When two tangents are exactly parallel, or so close to it that the old applet's |det| < 1 guard refused to draw, the status asks for another drag; no claim is made there.

The old applet picked its fourth dot at angle 4.5 but also computed a random angle it never used; this page starts at the four fixed angles so the opening picture is always the same. It uses a 400 by 250 board (the size the applet itself called optimal) instead of the 500 by 300 board of the archived page, and always labels the touch points although that page set ShowNames=0.

Drag one dot very close to its neighbour. One corner flies far away; press Check the theorem and watch the meeting dot stay with the four lines.
